section.title: The Discourse on the Church
section.sectionRationale: The fourth great discourse turns from Jesus' identity to the life of His community. Greatness is childlike humility, little ones must never be despised or made to stumble, the straying are sought, sin between brothers is addressed with patient discipline, and forgiveness among the forgiven has no limit.
section.thesis: In the community of the King, greatness is humble childlikeness, the least are precious and pursued, sin is confronted for the sake of restoration, and those forgiven an unpayable debt must forgive their brothers from the heart.
section.frameNote: Five beats: the greatest is the humble child; the gravity of causing little ones to stumble; the Father's pursuit of the straying sheep; confronting a sinning brother and the authority of the church; and the parable of the unforgiving servant.

verses.text: At that time the disciples came to Jesus and asked, “Who then is the greatest in the kingdom of heaven?”
Jesus invited a little child to stand among them.
“Truly I tell you,” He said, “unless you change and become like little children, you will never enter the kingdom of heaven.
Therefore, whoever {{tapeinoo|humbles}} himself like this little child is the greatest in the kingdom of heaven.
And whoever welcomes a little child like this in My name welcomes Me.

units.label: Causes of sin
units.note: woe to those who make little ones stumble

verses.text: But if anyone causes one of these little ones who believe in Me to stumble, it would be better for him to have a large millstone hung around his neck and to be drowned in the depths of the sea.
Woe to the world for the causes of sin. These stumbling blocks must come, but woe to the man through whom they come!
If your hand or your foot causes you to sin, cut it off and throw it away. It is better for you to enter life crippled or lame than to have two hands and two feet and be thrown into the eternal fire.
And if your eye causes you to sin, gouge it out and throw it away. It is better for you to enter life with one eye than to have two eyes and be thrown into the fire of hell.
See that you do not look down on any of these little ones. For I tell you that their angels in heaven always see the face of My Father in heaven.
What do you think? If a man has a hundred sheep and one of them goes astray, will he not leave the ninety-nine on the hills and go out to search for the one that is lost?
And if he finds it, truly I tell you, he rejoices more over that one sheep than over the ninety-nine that did not go astray.
In the same way, your Father in heaven is not willing that any of these little ones should perish.

units.label: A brother who sins
units.note: confront, restore, and the authority of the church

verses.text: If your brother sins against you, go and confront him privately. If he listens to you, you have won your brother over.
But if he will not listen, take one or two others along, so that ‘every matter may be established by the testimony of two or three witnesses.’
If he refuses to listen to them, tell it to the {{ekklesia|church}}. And if he refuses to listen even to the church, regard him as you would a pagan or a tax collector.
Truly I tell you, whatever you bind on earth will be bound in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth will be loosed in heaven.
Again, I tell you truly that if two of you on the earth agree about anything you ask for, it will be done for you by My Father in heaven.
For where two or three gather together in My name, there am I with them.”
Then Peter came to Jesus and asked, “Lord, how many times shall I forgive my brother who sins against me? Up to seven times?”
Jesus answered, “I tell you, not just seven times, but seventy-seven times!
Because of this, the kingdom of heaven is like a king who wanted to settle accounts with his servants.
As he began the settlements, a debtor owing ten thousand talents was brought to him.
Since the man was unable to pay, the master ordered that he be sold to pay his debt, along with his wife and children and everything he owned.
Then the servant fell on his knees before him. ‘Have patience with me,’ he begged, ‘and I will pay back everything.’
His master had compassion on him, {{aphiemi|forgave}} his debt, and released him.
But when that servant went out, he found one of his fellow servants who owed him a hundred denarii. He grabbed him and began to choke him, saying, ‘Pay back what you owe me!’
So his fellow servant fell down and begged him, ‘Have patience with me, and I will pay you back.’
But he refused. Instead, he went and had the man thrown into prison until he could pay his debt.
When his fellow servants saw what had happened, they were greatly distressed, and they went and recounted all of this to their master.
Then the master summoned him and said, ‘You wicked servant! I forgave all your debt because you begged me.
Shouldn’t you have had mercy on your fellow servant, just as I had on you?’
In anger his master turned him over to the jailers to be tortured, until he should repay all that he owed.
That is how My heavenly Father will treat each of you unless you forgive your brother from your heart.”

tapeinoo.gloss: To make low, to humble. Greatness in the kingdom is inverted: it belongs to the one who lowers himself like a small child, dependent and unassuming, rather than to the one who grasps for status.

ekklesia.gloss: The assembly, the church, the gathered community of Jesus' people. Here it is the body before which unrepented sin is finally brought, entrusted with the authority to bind and loose, that is, to affirm or withhold fellowship in Christ's name.

aphiemi.gloss: To send away, release, cancel, forgive. It is used both for the king cancelling the vast debt and for the forgiveness God's people owe one another; those released from an unpayable debt must release their brothers.

basic.context: The disciples ask who is greatest. Jesus sets a child among them and says greatness is childlike humility. He warns solemnly against causing little ones to stumble and against sin in ourselves. He tells of a shepherd who leaves ninety-nine to seek one stray, showing the Father's heart. He gives a process for confronting a sinning brother, and the church's authority to bind and loose. Then, answering Peter, He teaches limitless forgiveness through the parable of a servant forgiven a huge debt who refuses to forgive a small one.
basic.hermeneutics: This is the fourth of Matthew's five discourses, and it is about community life, not individual piety alone. Read the parts together: humility, protecting the vulnerable, seeking the stray, restoring the sinner, and forgiving without limit all flow from grace received. The parable's ending is a sober warning, not a denial of grace: those truly forgiven will forgive.
basic.originalLanguages: Greatness belongs to the one who tapeinoo, humbles himself like a child. Serious sin is brought at last before the ekklesia, the church, which binds and looses in Christ's name. And the whole chapter turns on aphiemi, to release or forgive, the vast debt cancelled by the king and the debts we owe each other.
basic.typology: The seeking shepherd fulfills God's promise in Ezekiel 34 to seek His scattered sheep Himself. The unpayable debt cancelled pictures the forgiveness of sins that the cross secures.
basic.christ: Jesus is the humble one who became a child and a servant, the Good Shepherd who leaves the ninety-nine to seek the one, and He is present wherever two or three gather in His name. The king's mercy in the parable is the mercy Jesus purchases.
basic.god: The Father does not will that one little one perish and rejoices over the found. He is the King who cancels an unpayable debt out of compassion, and He requires that the forgiven forgive, for a heart that refuses mercy has not truly received it.
basic.crossReferences: Ezekiel 34 promises God will seek His straying sheep. Deuteronomy 19 gives the two or three witnesses. Colossians 3 and Ephesians 4 call the forgiven to forgive as God forgave them. Luke 15 tells the lost sheep as joy over one repentant sinner.
basic.oneStory: Having revealed who He is, Jesus shapes the community He is building. Its greatness is humility, its care reaches the least and the straying, its discipline aims at restoration, and its air is forgiveness, because everyone in it has been forgiven a debt they could never pay. This is the family the crucified and risen King gathers, and it lives by the mercy it has received.

context.literary:
Matthew 18 is the fourth of the five great blocks of teaching in the Gospel, and it is the only one that is addressed chiefly to the disciples about their life with one another. The earlier discourses spoke of the kingdom's ethics, mission, parables and now, turning inward, its common life. The frame is the familiar Matthean formula that closes the discourse in 19:1, when Jesus had finished saying these things, the same sentence that closes each of the five.

The structure is a chain of linked sayings in which each unit grows from the last by a catchword. The child of verses 2 to 5 becomes the little ones of verses 6 and 10. The little ones who may be caused to stumble lead to the warning about the hand, the foot and the eye. The stray sheep of verses 12 to 14 returns to the language of the lost, and the brother who sins in verses 15 to 17 is the sheep in human form. The talk of binding and loosing leads to the promise of Jesus' presence, and Peter's question about how often to forgive leads to the parable that holds the whole together. The word brother runs like a thread through verses 15, 21, 35, and the verb to forgive, aphiemi, appears on both sides of the chapter.

Two small literary signals deserve notice. The parable in verses 23 to 34 is built on the number contrast of ten thousand against a hundred, and it is told in a three-act pattern, forgiveness, refusal, reversal. Verse 22 plays on Genesis 4:24, where Lamech boasted of vengeance seventy-sevenfold, so that Jesus sets a seventy-sevenfold forgiveness against the ancient seventy-sevenfold revenge. Finally, the bracketing is quiet but effective: the discourse starts with a question about who is greatest and ends with a king who comes to settle accounts, so that status and judgment frame the whole.
context.historical:
In the world of Jesus' hearers a child had no standing. Children were dependants with no legal claim and no social weight, so the child whom Jesus sets in the middle of the circle is not a symbol of innocence so much as of absence of status. The disciples are arguing about rank, and the answer is a person with none.

The millstone of verse 6 is not the small hand mill but the large stone turned by a donkey, the kind used in a village mill, and drowning in the depths of the sea was a death that left no grave. The valley of Hinnom outside Jerusalem, whose name stands behind the word translated hell, is where children were once burned to Molech, Jeremiah 7:31-32, and it became a picture of final judgment. The BSB notes in its footnote that the fire of hell is literally the Gehenna of fire.

The procedure of verses 15 to 17 comes straight out of the law. Leviticus 19:17 required a man to rebuke his neighbour directly and not to nurse hatred, and Deuteronomy 19:15 limited any accusation to the testimony of two or three witnesses. A community rule found among the Dead Sea scrolls also requires private reproof before witnesses, so the pattern was in the air. What is new in Jesus' teaching is the aim, to win your brother over, and the final step, the ekklesia, which in Matthew's Gospel appears only here and in Matthew 16:18.

The parable relies on real figures. A talent was worth about twenty years' wages for a laborer, as the BSB footnote says, so ten thousand talents is a debt of about two hundred thousand years of labour, a sum no household could ever have owed. A denarius was customarily a day's wage, so the fellow servant owes about a hundred days of labour. Selling a debtor with his family, verse 25, and imprisonment until payment, verse 30, were the realities of the debt law that Israel's own scripture tried to restrain, Leviticus 25:39-41 and Deuteronomy 15:1-2.
context.canonical:
The shepherd passage reaches back to Ezekiel 34, where God pronounces judgment on the shepherds of Israel who have scattered the flock and promises, I Myself will search for My flock and seek them out, Ezekiel 34:11. He will seek the lost, bring back the strays, bind up the broken and strengthen the weak, Ezekiel 34:16. Jeremiah 50:6 describes God's people as lost sheep led astray by their shepherds, and Isaiah 40:11 pictures the Lord gathering the lambs in His arms. Jesus places Himself in the role of the shepherd God promised to be. Luke 15:4-7 tells the same story with an emphasis on the joy over one repentant sinner, and John 10:11-16 adds that the shepherd lays down His life for the sheep. The apostle Peter writes that those who were like sheep going astray have returned to the Shepherd and Overseer of their souls, 1 Peter 2:25.

The teaching on binding and loosing is anchored by Matthew 16:19, where it is promised to Peter, and by Matthew 18:18, where it is given to the gathered community. The risen Lord gives a related commission when He says that those whose sins the disciples forgive are forgiven, John 20:23. The use of the two or three witnesses in verse 16 is Deuteronomy 19:15, and Paul uses the same principle for church discipline in 2 Corinthians 13:1 and 1 Timothy 5:19.

The call to forgive appears throughout the New Testament in the same terms as the parable. The Lord's Prayer asks forgive us our debts, as we also have forgiven our debtors, Matthew 6:12, and Jesus adds the warning that follows, Matthew 6:14-15. Paul tells the church to forgive as the Lord forgave you, Colossians 3:13, and Ephesians 4:32 uses the same pattern. Mark 9:42 gives the millstone warning in a parallel form, and Paul's pastoral treatment of a repentant offender in 2 Corinthians 2:6-8 shows the discourse applied.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Matthew arranged these sayings for a young community that was already finding that church life is hard. Some were jockeying for position, some were stumbling and some were hurting one another, and Matthew wanted to say how a people under the rule of Jesus handle those things. The discourse is a manual of conduct, but it is built on theology: every command rests on a statement about the Father. Humility rests on the fact that the child is received in Jesus' name, the pursuit of the stray rests on the Father's unwillingness that any perish, discipline rests on the presence of Jesus in the gathered community, and forgiveness rests on a debt already cancelled.

Matthew also means the reader to feel the weight of the little ones. Their angels, in verse 10, always see the face of the Father, which says that no believer is too small to be of concern in heaven. The warnings about stumbling are not exaggeration for effect; they are a way of saying that the cost of harming a believer is measured by the Father's love for the believer, not by the believer's importance.

The final parable is the interpretive key to the chapter. The question asked by Peter is about arithmetic, and the answer given is about the heart. By ending with from your heart, Matthew insists that forgiveness is not a ledger entry but a response to being forgiven.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
Most of this chapter is direct instruction, and it asks to be obeyed. Become like a child, do not cause a little one to stumble, go after the strays, confront privately, forgive. These are commands addressed to the disciples, and they carry over to the church in every age.

Some elements are hyperbole and picture. The cutting off of a hand or the gouging out of an eye in verses 8 and 9 is not literal instruction to maim oneself, and the early church never read it that way. It is a vivid way of saying that nothing, however precious, is worth keeping if it leads into sin, and it should be read in the same way as the similar saying in Matthew 5:29-30.

The procedure of verses 15 to 17 is prescriptive for the case it addresses, the sin of one believer against another, but it does not cover every sort of wrong. A case of abuse, for example, may rightly be taken straight to the proper authorities, and Paul handles a flagrant public sin in a different way, 1 Corinthians 5:4-5. The parable is partly description and partly warning, and its last sentence is a direct address to every hearer, each of you.

debates.question: Who are the little ones?

views.label: Literal children
views.case: The discourse begins with a child standing in the middle, verse 2, and the welcoming in verse 5 is of a little child. The little ones may then be actual children, who must not be led astray or despised.

views.label: Humble believers of any age
views.case: Verse 6 specifies little ones who believe in Me, and the term is used for disciples in Matthew 10:42. On this view the child is the model and the little ones are all who have taken that humble place, however old.

views.label: The weak, the vulnerable and the easily overlooked
views.case: The sheep that goes astray in verse 12 and the brother who sins in verse 15 suggest that the little ones include the wavering and the ones on the edge of the community.

debates.bearing: The views overlap. The text starts from a child and moves to believers who have taken that low place, and it requires that the community watch over its weakest members as the Father does.

debates.question: What do binding and loosing mean?

views.label: The authority to declare sins forgiven or retained
views.case: The saying is placed after the procedure for dealing with sin, and John 20:23 links the disciples' forgiving of sins with their being forgiven. On this view the church declares, on the basis of the gospel, whom God has received and whom He has not.

views.label: The authority to teach and decide questions of conduct
views.case: In Jewish usage to bind and to loose were terms for forbidding and permitting. The church's teaching under the apostles settles what is allowed and what is not, and Matthew 16:19 gives the same authority to Peter.

views.label: A discipline decision made in the presence of Christ
views.case: The context of verses 15 to 20 is a community decision on a particular sin, and the promise that Jesus is among two or three gives that decision His backing.

debates.bearing: Both the teaching and the declaring of forgiveness arise from the church's acting on what has already been decided in heaven. The Greek verbs in verse 18 are in a form that can be read as will have been bound and will have been loosed, which speaks of heaven's prior decision being followed, not heaven following ours.

debates.question: What does regard him as a pagan or a tax collector require?

views.label: Exclusion from the fellowship
views.case: The gentile and the tax collector were outsiders to the covenant community, and the passage ends with a person standing outside after refusing to hear the church. Paul orders something similar in 1 Corinthians 5:11-13.

views.label: Continuing outreach to someone outside
views.case: Matthew's Jesus is the friend of tax collectors and sinners, Matthew 11:19, and called a tax collector to follow Him, Matthew 9:9. To treat someone as a tax collector may mean continuing to seek him, not abandoning him.

debates.bearing: The two views belong together. The person is no longer treated as a member in good standing, yet he is treated as someone for whom the shepherd still searches. The aim of the whole process, restoring the brother, is not given up, and 2 Corinthians 2:6-8 shows the church welcoming an offender back.

debates.question: Does the unforgiving servant teach that a truly forgiven person can lose God's forgiveness?

views.label: A sober warning that reveals the heart
views.case: A persistent, hard refusal to forgive shows that a person never truly grasped or received God's mercy; the parable exposes a false, unregenerate heart rather than a genuinely forgiven one being unforgiven, consistent with justification by grace.

views.label: A real and serious threat of judgment
views.case: Jesus says plainly this is how the Father will treat each of you unless you forgive from the heart, and the church must feel the weight of that warning; unforgiveness is not a small thing but places one under judgment.

debates.bearing: Both agree that the forgiven must forgive and that unforgiveness is spiritually deadly. The passage works as a searching warning that drives the professing believer back to the mercy of God, not as a licence to presume on it.

study.originalLanguages:
The first verb to notice in verse 3 is strapheite, translated change and literally turn. Jesus asks the disciples to turn round, a word close to the idea of repentance, and the passive form suggests something that must happen to them. The goal is not to become childish but to become dependent and without a claim, which is why verse 4 speaks of humbling oneself and not simply of becoming young.

The verb for causing a stumble is skandalizo, from skandalon, originally the trigger of a trap and so an obstacle that makes someone fall. Matthew uses it of those who lose faith and of those who lead others astray, and it appears again in the tax scene of Matthew 17:27 where Jesus pays so as not to cause offence. The millstone in verse 6 is a large one, literally a donkey millstone, in contrast to a small hand mill. The picture is of a drowning that cannot be undone.

In the parable of the sheep the verb to go astray, planao, is used in verses 12 and 13, the same verb used in 1 Peter 2:25 for people who were like sheep going astray. The sheep is not malicious; it has been led astray and wandered. Verse 14 says the Father is not willing, literally that it is not the will, thelema, of your Father that one of these should perish. The verb perish, apollymi, is the same word used for the lost sheep.

In verse 15 the verb translated won over is kerdaino, literally to gain. The goal of private confrontation is not victory in an argument but gaining a person. Verse 17 uses ekklesia for the church, a word that in the Greek Old Testament often translates the Hebrew qahal, the assembly of God's people, so Jesus calls His gathering the assembly in a way that gives it the dignity of Israel's own.

In verse 18 the verbs for binding and loosing are in a form that can be read as a future perfect passive, will have been bound, will have been loosed. The grammar has often been taken to say that heaven's decision precedes the church's action. Verse 19 uses symphoneo for agree, the origin of our word symphony, meaning to sound together, the same verb used in Matthew 20:2 of the agreement between the landowner and the workers.

In the parable the word translated compassion in verse 27 is splanchnistheis, from splanchna, the inner parts, the seat of feeling. It is the same verb Matthew uses of Jesus' own compassion, Matthew 20:34. The master's mercy is the Lord's own. The sum of ten thousand is a myriad, the largest single number in Greek, which makes the contrast with a hundred denarii rhetorical as well as numerical. In verse 34 the jailers are basanistai, those who inflict torment, which is a stern word for the consequence the unforgiving servant brings upon himself.

Finally, seventy-seven times in verse 22 can also be read as seventy times seven, as the BSB footnote says, and the phrase echoes Genesis 4:24 in the Greek Old Testament. Either way the sense is not to count.

typology.type: The shepherd who seeks the scattered flock, Ezekiel 34:11-16
typology.fulfillment: In Ezekiel the LORD condemns the shepherds who have fed themselves and scattered the flock, and then promises that He Himself will search for His sheep, rescue them, bind up the broken and bring back the strays. In Jesus the promise is carried out in person. He leaves the ninety-nine and goes after the one, Luke 15:4-7, and says He lays down His life for the sheep, John 10:11. Hebrews 13:20 calls Him the great Shepherd of the sheep. The type falls short in that the earlier shepherd rescued from exile, while Christ rescues from sin and death, and He is both the Shepherd and the one who dies for the flock.

Lamech boasted that if Cain was avenged sevenfold, he would be avenged seventy-sevenfold, the first song of escalating violence in Scripture. Jesus takes up the very number and turns it round: the answer to Peter is seventy-seven times of forgiveness, verse 22. The correspondence reverses the old curse by pouring out grace in the same measure. Paul states the same in Romans 12:19-21, which refuses vengeance and overcomes evil with good. The pattern falls short only in that the number is not a quota, and the real fulfilment is the cross, where God absorbs the debt Himself.

typology.type: The release of debts in the seventh year, Deuteronomy 15:1-2
typology.fulfillment: Israel was told that every seventh year creditors must release what a neighbour owed, a built-in rhythm of cancelled debt. Peter's offer of seven times unknowingly echoes that rhythm, and Jesus' seventy-seven stretches it to every day. The king's cancelling of the vast debt acts out the release in its fullest form. Luke records Jesus proclaiming release to the captives in Nazareth, Luke 4:18, and Colossians 2:13-14 says that God cancelled the record of debt that stood against us, nailing it to the cross. The type falls short because the old release returned debts to the books after a time, and Christ's release is final.

typology.type: God's dwelling among His people, Exodus 25:8
typology.fulfillment: God told Israel to make a sanctuary so that He might dwell among them, and the tent of meeting was the place where a matter could be brought before Him. Jesus says that where two or three gather in His name, He is with them, verse 20. The Gospel begins with Immanuel, God with us, Matthew 1:23, and ends with the promise I am with you always, Matthew 28:20. The tent's mercy seat is replaced by a person who is present wherever His people meet, and the correspondence is that the church is now the place of His presence, 1 Corinthians 3:16. The type falls short in that the tent stood in one place and was entered by one man once a year.

study.christ:
Jesus is first the pattern of the childlikeness He asks for. The disciples ask who is greatest, and the Son of God, who has every right to be great, takes a place lower than they do. Paul's hymn says that He did not consider equality with God something to be grasped, but emptied Himself and humbled Himself to death on a cross, Philippians 2:6-8. The verb Matthew uses for humbling in verse 4 is the verb Paul uses in Philippians 2:8. The greatness Jesus commends is the greatness He lives.

Second, He is the Shepherd who does what God promised in Ezekiel 34. The shepherd of the parable does not wait for the lost sheep to find its way back, and Jesus says later that the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost, Luke 19:10. The BSB footnote to verse 10 notes that some manuscripts add this sentence as verse 11, and whether or not it belongs here, the thought runs through the whole passage. The shepherd goes where the strays are. The Good Shepherd lays down His life for the sheep, John 10:11, and this is where the picture exceeds every earlier shepherd.

Third, He is the living centre of the gathered community. The promise that where two or three gather in My name, there am I with them, verse 20, is the claim of a person who shares the presence of God. It is the middle of a Gospel that begins with God with us and ends with I am with you always. A church is not a club, or only a school of ethics, but the gathering in which the risen Lord is present.

Fourth, He is the ground of the parable. The king who cancels a debt of ten thousand talents is not Jesus under another face, and care is needed not to turn the parable into a code. Yet the debt that no servant could pay is the debt Jesus will pay. He gives His life as a ransom for many, Matthew 20:28, and the blood of the covenant is poured out for the forgiveness of sins, Matthew 26:28. The forgiveness the forgiven are asked to extend flows from a forgiveness that cost the Son His life.

Finally, He is the one who bears the exact thing the warning describes. He was handed over, tortured and put to death, and He did not demand payment from those who owed Him. On the cross He prays for those who crucify Him, Luke 23:34, and Peter's question about seventy-seven times is answered in the life of the Lord Peter would one day deny and be forgiven by.
study.god:
The God of this chapter is first of all a Father who cares about individuals. The statement that it is not the Father's will that any of the little ones should perish, verse 14, is a statement about the heart of God. The shepherd's leaving of the ninety-nine is not carelessness but a picture of a love that does not treat any one of its own as expendable. The Father's attention to the little ones, whose angels always see His face, verse 10, shows that He is not distracted by the great and the powerful. Hebrews 1:14 says that angels are ministering spirits sent to serve those who will inherit salvation, and the angels of the little ones are the Father's way of saying that heaven's gaze rests on the least.

The chapter also shows God as a King who keeps accounts. The parable says plainly that the master wants to settle accounts, and the debt is real. God does not pretend that sin is small. The chapter holds the severity of the debt, ten thousand talents, together with the generosity of the cancellation. Psalm 130:3-4 says that if the LORD kept track of iniquities no one could stand, but there is forgiveness with Him. The king's mercy is not a lowering of standards but a payment taken on himself, which the New Testament will reveal in the cross.

A tension runs through the passage that must not be resolved too quickly. The master is tender in verse 27 and angry in verse 34. The Father is not willing that any should perish, and yet He will treat the unforgiving as the master did. God is infinitely forbearing and does not take mercy lightly. These are not two moods but one holiness, which is why the forgiven are asked to forgive and not to hold their own small debts over others.

For worship the discourse offers a few clear lessons. We come to God as little ones and not as great ones, and we come as people who have been forgiven what we could never repay. A congregation shaped by this chapter will welcome the unimportant, seek the drifting, rebuke in love and forgive from the heart. Prayer is said to be heard when two agree, verse 19, because it is prayer within a community that Jesus is present in. The worship the chapter asks for is a common life in which the character of the Father shows.

crossReferences.note: God promises that He Himself will search for His scattered flock, seek the lost, bring back the strays and bind up the broken. The shepherd of Jesus' parable is this promise in person, and the Father's will that none perish is the same compassion.

Luke tells the same sheep story with an emphasis on the joy of finding. There is more joy in heaven over one sinner who repents than over ninety-nine righteous ones who need no repentance. Reading it beside Matthew shows that the Father's unwillingness for any to perish is matched by His rejoicing when one returns.

The law told an Israelite not to harbour hatred but to rebuke his neighbour directly so as not to incur guilt. The first step of Jesus' procedure, go and confront him privately, deepens that law by making restoration, and not mere clearing of one's own guilt, the goal.

A matter must be established by the testimony of two or three witnesses. Jesus quotes this rule in verse 16 as the reason for taking one or two others along, protecting the accused from a single voice and the accuser from a mere private grudge.

The earlier promise of the keys of the kingdom to Peter, with the same words about binding and loosing. In Matthew 18:18 the authority is given to the whole community, so Peter's confession and the church built on it are the context for church discipline.

Lamech boasts of seventy-sevenfold revenge, and Jesus answers Peter with seventy-seven times of forgiveness, verse 22. The reversal sets the ethic of the kingdom against the first escalation of violence in the Bible.

The Lord's Prayer asks that our debts be forgiven as we forgive our debtors, and the parable acts out that petition. Matthew 6:14-15 adds the warning that the Father will not forgive those who do not forgive, which is what the parable's last verse repeats.

Paul tells the church to bear with one another and to forgive as the Lord forgave you. The measure of Christian forgiveness is the Lord's own forgiveness, which is the logic of the king's question, shouldn't you have had mercy as I had on you.

Christ Jesus emptied Himself and humbled Himself to the point of death on a cross. The same humbling Jesus commends to the disciples in verse 4 is what He Himself does, so the pattern of the child is the pattern of the Lord.

Jesus says He is the good shepherd who lays down His life for the sheep, and that He has other sheep to bring in. The seeking shepherd of Matthew 18 is made explicit as a person whose seeking costs His life.

Jesus praises the Father because the things of the kingdom are hidden from the wise and revealed to little children. It explains why a child is the model of the kingdom and why the little ones matter so much to the Father.

Paul shows church discipline in action: the assembled church, in the name of Jesus, hands over a man in flagrant sin with the aim of his salvation on the Day of the Lord. It illustrates both the seriousness and the restorative purpose of Matthew 18:17.

study.oneStory:
The Bible's first great division among people is a division by vengeance. Cain kills Abel, and Lamech sings of seventy-sevenfold revenge. The story of Scripture is, among other things, the story of how that escalating violence is answered. God answers Cain's crime by setting a protecting mark on him, Genesis 4:15, and His chosen people are formed by an exodus out of slavery and a law that tells them to release their debtors every seventh year. The prophets, though, keep saying that Israel's leaders have failed to shepherd, and Ezekiel hears God say that He Himself will do it.

Matthew 18 is where that promise is lived out in the life of a community. Jesus sets the model of the child in the circle, and the kingdom is entered by those who have no claim. The shepherd goes out for the one, and a church whose discipline aims to win a brother is a church shaped by the Father who is not willing that anyone perish. The first act of forgiveness in the passage is not the believers' but the king's, and everything follows from that. The debt that no one can pay is cancelled, and the cancelled person is asked to pass on what he has received.

The chapter sets up what follows. In the next chapters the road to Jerusalem gets steeper, and the cancelling of the debt will be paid for by the Son of Man giving His life as a ransom for many, Matthew 20:28. The community of the discourse is the community that will be born of that death, which is why Jesus promises His presence in it and gives it the authority to bind and loose. After the resurrection the same promise appears as the closing line of the Gospel, I am with you always, Matthew 28:20.

The story ends in a new creation in which no one is left outside through unforgiveness. Revelation 21:3 hears a voice say that the dwelling of God is with men, and 21:4 says He will wipe away every tear. The community that learned to forgive from the heart in the shadow of the cross becomes the city in which the Lamb is the lamp, and in which the little ones, with their angels, see the face of the Father.

quiz.q: How does Jesus define greatness in the kingdom?

options.text: Humbling oneself like a little child, low and dependent.
options.note: Verses 3-4 make childlike humility the mark of greatness.

options.text: Serving others in visible acts of ministry.
options.note: Service flows from it, but Jesus points to humility itself, becoming like a child, as the root.

options.text: Gaining influence and authority over others.
options.note: That is the disciples' assumption, which Jesus overturns.

options.text: Achieving the most in religious accomplishment.
options.note: Jesus commends lowliness, not accomplishment, as the path to greatness.

quiz.q: What does the parable of the lost sheep reveal about the Father?

options.text: He seeks the straying and is not willing that even one little one should perish.
options.note: Verses 12-14 show God's pursuing, rejoicing heart.

options.text: He cares about the whole flock and keeps them safe.
options.note: True, but the point is His pursuit of the single stray, which this general statement misses.

options.text: He is content to keep the ninety-nine and let the one go.
options.note: The opposite; He leaves the ninety-nine to search for the one.

options.text: He judges the stray for wandering away.
options.note: He seeks and rejoices over the stray rather than judging it.

quiz.q: What is the goal of confronting a sinning brother?

options.text: To win him back through patient, escalating steps, restoration not rejection.
options.note: Verses 15-17 aim first at winning the brother, involving the church only if he refuses.

options.text: To gather enough witnesses to prove he is guilty.
options.note: Witnesses are involved, but they serve restoration, not merely proving guilt.

options.text: To remove troublesome people from the church quickly.
options.note: The process is deliberately patient and aims at repentance, not swift removal.

options.text: To publicly shame the offender before everyone.
options.note: It begins privately and seeks to win the brother, not to shame him.

quiz.q: What is the main point of the parable of the unforgiving servant?

options.text: Those forgiven an unpayable debt by God must forgive their brothers from the heart.
options.note: Verses 32-35 tie our forgiveness of others to the mercy we have received.

options.text: We should forgive others a set number of times, like seventy-seven.
options.note: The number pictures limitless forgiveness, not a literal count, which this misreads.

options.text: God expects us to repay our debts to Him fully.
options.note: The debt is unpayable and cancelled by grace; the point is mercy, not repayment.

options.text: Forgiveness is optional for those who follow Jesus.
options.note: Jesus makes heartfelt forgiveness essential, not optional, for the forgiven.

quiz.q: What is promised where two or three gather in Jesus' name?

options.text: Jesus Himself is present among them.
options.note: Verse 20 promises His personal presence with the gathered community.

options.text: Their prayers will always get exactly what they ask.
options.note: There is a promise about agreed prayer, but the climax is His presence, and prayer is according to the Father's will.

options.text: They will have authority to do whatever they wish.
options.note: The authority to bind and loose serves Christ's purposes; it is not unlimited self-will.

options.text: A large crowd is needed for Jesus to be present.
options.note: Even two or three suffice; His presence is not a matter of numbers.

questions: Jesus set a child in the middle and called that greatness. Where is your desire for status quietly at odds with the humility He commends?
The Father seeks the one who strays. Is there someone drifting from Christ whom you have written off but God is still pursuing, perhaps through you?
Jesus gives careful steps for confronting sin, aimed at winning a brother. Where have you either avoided a needed conversation or handled one without love?
You have been forgiven a debt you could never repay. What grudge are you still holding that this mercy calls you to release?
Forgiveness here is from the heart, not just the lips. What would it look like to forgive someone deeply this week rather than merely tolerating them?

translationNotes.note: The BSB numbering goes from verse 10 to verse 12; verse 11, for the Son of Man came to save the lost, is not in the earliest manuscripts and appears as a footnote drawn from Luke 19:10.
The phrase may be rendered seventy-seven times or seventy times seven; either way it signifies limitless forgiveness, deliberately reversing Lamech's boast of unlimited vengeance in Genesis 4:24.
Ten thousand talents was an almost unimaginable sum, a talent being about twenty years' wages; the debt is designed to be unpayable, dwarfing the hundred denarii owed by the fellow servant.
